title: A flat fee to speak up
allegory: The L1 penalty is like a flat fee for speaking at a committee: every unit of talk costs the same, so members with only a small point say exactly nothing, and the size of the fee decides whether the committee is silent, chatty or usefully brief.
map: a flat fee for every unit of speech
speak only if your point is worth more than the fee
f = max(0, a − λ): evidence below λ gives exactly zero
fee too high: some never speak again; too low: everyone chatters

cap.1: Ask a big committee to describe one sentence and everyone talks at once. True, but useless. You want the few voices that matter.
cap.2: An SAE rewrites an activation as a mix of many latent directions. With no pressure it uses lots of them at once, and nothing is readable.
cap.3: An overcomplete dictionary admits infinitely many exact decompositions of x. A prior must select a sparse one; the L1 penalty is the classic choice.

props.label: fee: λ per unit of talk

cap.1: Charge a flat fee for every word spoken. Now a member only speaks if their point is worth more than the fee, and most stay completely silent.
cap.2: The loss becomes reconstruction error + λ × (sum of all latent activations). Every unit of activation costs λ, so latents stay at zero unless they earn their keep.
cap.3: L = ‖x − x̂‖² + λ Σᵢ fᵢ, with fᵢ ≥ 0 after the ReLU so |fᵢ| = fᵢ. λ is the exchange rate between reconstruction error and activation mass.

cap.1: Two costs, added: how badly the committee's summary rebuilds the sentence, plus the fee times all the talking. λ sets the fee.
cap.2: Reconstruction loss keeps latents honest; the L1 term keeps them quiet. λ is the single dial between the two, and the biggest lever in SAE training.
cap.3: The L1 coefficient trades reconstruction against sparsity. Read sparsity as L0, the mean number of non-zero latents per token.

curves.label: L1 fee: exact zeros below λ

cap.1: How loudly a member speaks against how much they have to say. With a flat fee, anyone below the fee says exactly nothing; above it, they speak a bit quieter.
cap.2: For one latent the best activation is max(0, evidence − λ): a dead zone below λ, then shifted down by λ. A squared (L2) penalty only scales activations, so they never reach zero.
cap.3: The L1 proximal step is soft thresholding, f* = max(0, a − λ): exact zeros plus shrinkage of survivors. L2's gradient λf vanishes near 0, so it never yields exact zeros.

chapters.name: Too high, too low

left.title: λ too high
lines: dead latents: no gradient, lost for good

right.title: λ too low
lines: dense latents, fire on over 1 token in 100

chapters.verdict: Tune λ by watching L0, dead and dense counts together.

cap.1: Set the fee too high and some members never speak again. Too low and everyone chatters about everything. Neither committee explains anything.
cap.2: High λ gives dead latents that never fire, get no gradient and stay dead. Low λ gives dense, polysemantic ones. L1 warm-up exists because λ is hard to set from step one.
cap.3: Watch L0 (GemmaScope picked SAEs near L0 = 100; above 200 on a 1L TinyStories model suggests λ is too small), dead counts, and log-sparsity massed between about −5 and −3.

chapters.name: The fee is debated

right.title: newer: JumpReLU, TopK
lines: a threshold, or a fixed number of speakers
sparser is not always more readable

chapters.verdict: Learn L1's trade-off; expect to load JumpReLU or TopK SAEs too.

cap.1: People still argue about the best way to charge the fee. The flat fee works; newer schemes set a threshold or a fixed number of speakers instead.
cap.2: Current method in ARENA: ReLU + L1. Newer SAEs swap it for JumpReLU (GemmaScope) or TopK. What you need: the trade-off, and how to read L0, dead and dense latents.
cap.3: L1 couples sparsity with shrinkage; JumpReLU and TopK control sparsity more directly. Evaluation is unsolved: absorption and splitting mean sparser is not reliably more interpretable.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: λ decides how readable the dictionary is
Dead or dense: both waste the SAE
Readable latents are what you steer with

cap.1: This one dial decides whether an SAE gives you a readable list of what the model is thinking about, which is what you need to understand and steer it.
cap.2: SAE latents are what you inspect on Neuronpedia and clamp to steer, like the Golden Gate Bridge feature. Whether they are readable starts with this penalty.
cap.3: Sparsity is the inductive bias that makes dictionary latents candidate features; its strength sets the reconstruction/interpretability frontier every downstream analysis inherits.

coda.title: Set the fee and see who still speaks

params.label: penalty: 0 = L1 flat fee, 1 = L2 squared

readouts.label: committee
readouts.f: (() => { const n = [2.6, 1.9, 1.2, 0.8, 0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05].map(a => mode < 0.5 ? max(0, a - lam) : a / (1 + lam)).filter(f => f > 1e-9).length; return n === 0 ? 'silent: nothing rebuilt' : n >= 7 ? 'dense: nearly everyone talks' : 'sparse: a few clear voices'; })()

caption.1: Slide the fee up: quiet latents drop to exactly zero while loud ones survive, a bit quieter. Switch to the squared penalty and nobody ever goes fully silent.
caption.2: Each bar is one latent's activation after the fee, max(0, evidence − λ). L0 falls as λ rises and reconstruction error climbs. Under L2 everything shrinks and L0 stays at 8.
caption.3: Soft thresholding: exact zeros below λ, survivors shrunk by λ, the shrinkage JumpReLU and TopK avoid. L2 rescales by 1/(1 + λ), dense forever. Latents silent on every input die.

where_else: Lasso regression: the same flat penalty picks out a few features in statistics
Transcoders, which learn an MLP's input-to-output map under the same sparsity pressure
Compressed sensing: recovering a sparse signal from few measurements
Weight pruning, where a flat penalty drives whole weights to zero

hamming.what: The term λ·Σ|fᵢ| in an SAE's loss that charges for every unit of latent activation, pushing most latents to exactly zero.
hamming.when: Whenever you train a sparse autoencoder, or judge one by its L0, dead and dense counts.
hamming.why: It is the single dial between faithful reconstruction and a short, readable list of active latents.

object.title: The creased bowl
object.subtitle: A marble choosing how loudly two latents speak; the fee carves creases along the axes where a latent falls silent.

cap.1: Two latents, one bowl. With no fee the marble settles where both speak: the best rebuild.
cap.2: Reconstruction loss over two latent activations; minimum at (1.2, 0.5).
cap.3: ½‖a − f‖² with evidence a = (1.2, 0.5); the unpenalised optimum is f = a.

cap.1: Charge the fee. The bowl grows a crease along each axis, and the marble slides into one: latent 2 goes silent.
cap.2: λ = 0.6 with L1 moves the minimum to (0.6, 0). One latent is exactly zero.
cap.3: Soft thresholding per coordinate: f* = max(0, a − λ) = (0.6, 0). The kink at 0 is what captures the optimum.

cap.1: From above, the contours turn diamond-shaped with corners on the axes, so the lowest point sits on an axis.
cap.2: L1 contours have corners on the axes, and optima tend to land there. That is sparsity.
cap.3: The L1 ball's vertices lie on the coordinate axes, so penalised optima are generically sparse.

cap.1: Swap to a squared penalty: the bowl stays smooth and the marble stops short of the axis. Both latents keep murmuring.
cap.2: L2 at the same λ puts the minimum near (0.55, 0.23): shrunk, but never zero.
cap.3: Ridge shrinkage f* = a/(1 + 2λ): smooth, no kink, no exact zeros. L2 cannot produce sparse codes.

cap.1: Fee too high and the marble rolls to the corner: nobody speaks. Latents that never fire get no gradient, so they die.
cap.2: λ above both evidences gives f* = (0, 0). Across a dataset, this is how dead latents appear.
cap.3: λ ≥ max aᵢ zeroes everything; latents inactive on all inputs get zero gradient through the ReLU and stay dead.

predict.q: Why does an L1 penalty give exact zeros when an L2 penalty does not?

options.t: L1 pushes with the same force all the way to zero; L2's push fades as values shrink
L1 is simply a stronger penalty

predict.why: L1's gradient is a constant λ; L2's is λ·f, which vanishes near zero.

predict.q: L0 is 300 on a small one-layer model. What does that suggest?

options.t: λ is probably too small: the latents are dense

predict.why: An L0 above 200 on a 1L TinyStories model is almost certainly a too-small L1 coefficient.

predict.q: A high L1 coefficient mostly risks which failure?
predict.why: High L1 kills latents; low L1 lets them go dense. Warm-up schedules exist because the coefficient is hard to set from the start.

object.where: Anywhere a flat penalty buys exact zeros: lasso regression, compressed sensing, pruning.
